The Santa Cruz long-toed salamander (Ambystoma macrodactylum croceum) is known from only two sites both near Santa Cruz on the coast of California and isolated by 100 miles from another subspecies of Ambystoma macrodactylum. Threatened development of both breeding ponds as well as potential destruction of the chaparral woodlands where the salamander spends the remainder of the year must be avoided. Successful protection and management of the Santa Cruz salamander will not appreciably change its present restricted distribution.
The Florida manatee cannot tolerate cold temperatures and for that reason its range in the United States was always restricted to the South Atlantic and Gulf Coasts. Because of destruction and alteration of its habitat as well as hunting and wanton slaughter, it has been compressed today into a much smaller range confined to lower Florida. Potentially it could be restored to the remainder of Florida and for some distance up the Atlantic and around the Gulf Coasts.
While water seems to frequently be a factor limiting distribution of some species, there are other causes for geographical isolation. Some time in the geological past the Attwater's greater prairie chicken became isolated on the Gulf Coastal prairie of Texas far removed from the Northern greater prairie chicken of the vast tall grass prairies of Mid-America. Their ranges, both grassland, were separated by arms of the temperate deciduous forest biome. Both subspecies have been persecuted by conversion of their native grasslands to agricultural crops and by over-grazing until today the Attwater's is confined to a small area in 12 counties of coastal Texas.

Less than 2,000 birds remain. Successful restoration of the subspecies by protection and management of habitat could return it to selected areas from Southwest Learnana on the Gulf Coast to the success River in Texas.
